This study presents a novel dynamic modeling approach called TD-PAR, a time-dependent Poisson autoregressive model with cross-section and time effects, intended for analyzing and forecasting count-based data over time, particularly suitable for applications in economics, finance, and social sciences. A key advantage of TD-PAR is its capability to account for both cross-sectional and temporal variations when seeking optimal parameter estimates, thereby requiring a significantly reduced number of observations compared to traditional methods. A function is also introduced to compute the optimal initial values for estimating TD-PAR's parameters using a fixed-point iteration method, ensuring convergence without compromise. A method is also proposed to evaluate the goodness of fit for observed data when using TD-PAR. A comparison with an existing similar model demonstrates TD-PAR's enhanced forecasting performance and its ability to model conditional mean and variance dynamics when analyzing real-world data.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

A new molecular sampling method called RCD-LD is introduced and optimized for configuring polymers in a simulation. Building upon previous work, this method combines reaction coordinates and Langevin dynamics to efficiently explore conformational space. The authors compute reaction coordinate drift terms using numerical differentiation and implement the method using a widely accepted simulation package, ASE. To determine the method's parameters, the authors conduct extensive optimizations using a critical polynomial model. Subsequent Monte Carlo simulations are performed to determine the optimal reaction coordinate function, which results in a nearly unbiased configuration distribution. The paper's findings are confirmed by comparing the RCD-LD simulations with existing data on polymer configurations. The authors further validate the method by simulating polymer collapse induced by temperature changes and analyzing the resulting configuration distributions. The results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in sampling conformational space, especially for complex polymers, and its potential applications in biopolymer research.

Human-generated descriptions of images, commonly used to train and test image description systems, undergo evaluation to assess system performance. Recently, research has utilized benchmarks consisting of human descriptions to improve image description models, which have shown significant improvements. Our investigation examines the current state of human benchmarks, analyzing how they are acquired, evaluated, and utilized in image description systems. We further discuss the implications of using these benchmarks, highlighting how they might compromise privacy and pose technical challenges for disability access.

A novel approach has been taken to explore the connection between conformal field theory and Euler-Arnold equations. Beginning with the observation that certain nonlinear partial differential equations, specifically those of Euler-Arnold type, exhibit remarkable properties when transformed under a local conformal map, we then delve into analyzing how this transformation impacts Fock space over a massless scalar field. Specifically, we examine how local conformal transformations affect the Weyl anomaly coefficients as well as the Hamiltonian formulation of the theory, taking care to account for variations in the domain that are diffeomorphic. What results is a comprehensive picture of how the structure of Euler-Arnold equations emerges in conformal field theory, particularly in the massless scalar field scenario, offering a framework for classifying such structures based on topological characteristics of a given domain.

Using an extended lattice QCD setup that includes dynamical quarks, we perform a prediction of several new or previously undiscovered hadrons consisting of light quarks. These predictions take the form of mass estimates for particular hadron categories: a new vector resonance similar to the rho, a positively charged baryon with the configuration SSÂ¯, and a negatively charged baryon with the configuration TTÂ¯. We base these predictions on our existing knowledge of quark masses and their relationship to hadron properties, specifically the meson and baryon mass spectra. To determine these predictions, we utilize a chiral effective theory called ChPT, specifically its third-order implementation in a lattice QCD context that factors in 2+1 flavor dynamics. We also review the underlying theoretical framework, particularly the relevant ChPT formulas, to provide a comprehensive prediction for these new hadrons.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDED systems, where data and energy are jointly transmitted using multiple subcarriers and antennas. We derive the optimal wideband WF policy that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver, considering both fixed and fading channels. Additionally, we investigate the statistical properties of the received signal noise ratio, analyzing its average value and second moment for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM scenarios.

Determining proton profile functions, specifically their asymmetric variations, is a complex task that involves numerous theoretical and experimental components. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates proton parton density functions' determination and their application in perturbative QCD, specifically for the strong interaction constant's beta function. This revised approach enables the precise calculation of PDF errors, particularly when deriving limits on proton PDFs' unusual shapes, such as polarized protons. The paper's scope also extends to the development of a suitable model that facilitates the convergence of 2-to-n-loop PDF beta functions, reducing their derivation time, particularly for (n)CFT-like scenarios, when 2-to-n-loop contributions become significant.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame reacting to acoustic vibrations using an active reaction model, without relying on an RANS turbulence model, and utilizes a linearized Euler-Lagrange approach to describe gas-phase dynamics. Contrary to conventional linear methods, this active reaction model enables the reaction rate to respond to fluctuations in temperature and strain rate. To account for turbulence effects, a linearized anisotropic WALE model is employed to compute flame instability and interaction with acoustic waves. A combustion model is also used in its linear form to determine reaction rate fluctuations. Combining these elements allows for the simulation of acoustic resonance phenomena in a jet flame, revealing the formation of hot spots that can lead to flame extinction, as well as the disappearance of certain harmonic resonances in certain situations. The results obtained are further compared to DNS data, demonstrating the effectiveness of the presented methodology in predicting resonance behavior.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Its basic framework consists of a Poisson equation similar to Einstein's equation, but with a nonlocal operator that can be described as a memory function. The memory function contains valuable information about the physical properties of the system when the system is in a steady state. Nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to study various physical phenomena, including the behavior of shear waves in a gravitational field and the relationship between mass and gravity. The theory also enables the prediction of gravitational shear waves behavior when a shear stress induces a deformation in a system. When studying nonlocal effects, a constitutive relation similar to the one in nonlocal elasticity is necessary. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to study physical phenomena in a gravitational field, and it is analogous to nonlocal elasticity theory in an electromagnetic field. The memory function of the nonlocal gravity theory is comparable to the nonlocality parameter in nonlocal elasticity theory, and it can be further analyzed using the Laplace transform. The theoretical framework of nonlocal gravity theory is comparable to the framework of nonlocal elasticity theory, and it can be applied to study physical phenomena in a gravitational field.

This paper discusses the potential uses of minor systems in the LHC, particularly in conjunction with the main detectors. Since the main detectors will focus on the 100 TeV collisions, we propose utilizing smaller detectors to analyze events resulting from ncnc collisions, which produce heavier particles more frequently. We outline the possible roles of these minor systems, including their placement, functions, and proposed physics goals, with a focus on discovering heavy composites through compositeness signatures. We also explore the technical requirements for these systems, emphasizing the need for low-mass baryon and meson identification capabilities. Finally, we provide a framework for the minor systems' contribution to the LHC plan, suggesting a phased approach with incremental upgrades to accommodate various physics objectives.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries, when in a transient state, experience outbursts more frequently than black hole binaries. This idea is based on an assumption that a key factor influencing the frequency of outburst recurrence in these binaries is the nature of their compact object (either black hole or neutron star). Contrary to this idea, our research found that the recurrence intervals of neutron star binaries and black hole binaries are similar when considering a standard distance modulus, and the population of black holes in the Galactic center is unlikely to exceed 10,000. Moreover, our findings suggest that the recurrence interval of these binaries is primarily influenced by their binary system characteristics, particularly the mass of their neutron star or black hole, rather than its nature.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

As energy efficiency continues to pose a challenge in CPU design, a novel concept called HyperThreading has emerged. By implementing multiple low-frequency cores within a single high-frequency core, hyper-threading seeks to find an optimal balance between performance and power consumption. In this research, we propose a new hyper-threading architecture called HyperDegrade, which features multiple low-frequency cores that operate at a significantly lower frequency than the high-frequency core. To fully leverage the potential of this design, a new scheduling algorithm called DEGRADED-FIRST-COME-FIRST-SERVED (DFCFS) is also proposed. Through comprehensive evaluations using real-world workloads and applications, our findings indicate that HyperDegrade can achieve improved performance and energy efficiency compared to current hyper-threading designs. Specifically, our results show that HyperDegrade can deliver performance gains of up to 13.4x and energy reductions of up to 90x when executing single-threaded workloads. Furthermore, our data suggests that HyperDegrade outperforms the state-of-the-art hyper-threading architecture, called EWC, in terms of performance and energy efficiency, with performance improvements of up to 4.3x and energy reductions of up to 80x for multi-threaded workloads.

In the realm of knot theory, a key tool for analyzing knot projections is the disentangling move. It helps transform a knot diagram into its simplest form, which is a diagram representing a link composed of arcs and loops, without any crossings that form an oval shape. A refined invariant called the Khovanov homology can be computed from knot diagrams, and its properties suggest that a more sophisticated analysis of projection diagrams is necessary. Specifically, it is essential to define a operation that would remove a crossing of an S-kind, as only then can a function be defined that behaves well when applied to the knot projection diagram and the reduced diagram form. A new operation called "delta" meets this requirement, which in some cases allows for the computation of Khovanov homology for a given knot diagram more efficiently than the standard disentangling move.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination and decision-making can be critical tasks. We investigate a scenario where agents, capable of communication and computation, make strategic choices to achieve a common goal. If the agents' actions are visible to each other, they may face a dilemma where self-interest conflicts with the goal of cooperation. We examine a multi-task scenario where agents choose between two actions, each with a probability associated, to optimize their payoffs while contributing to the overall well-being of the system. The structure of the payoffs is key in determining the optimal collaborative strategy, which we term "collaborative equilibrium". We identify a set of graph configurations that allow for a collaborative equilibrium when the nodes are interconnected randomly. Furthermore, we analyze a linear payoff matrix and an arbitrary nonlinear one to determine the collaborative equilibrium when the graph topology is known in advance. If the graph structure is uncertain, we apply a learning algorithm to discover the collaborative equilibrium through exploration and exploitation of possible graph topologies.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group can be effectively incorporated into the wreath products of their respective actions on that set. This achievement enables us to illustrate the chain of subgroup embeddings with precise detail, serving as a key component in the proof of our main result, which predicts the potential subgroup embedding patterns based on given conditions.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are susceptible to blockage, which can create distinct, non-overlapping areas within their range that are unaffected by blockage. Research on the distribution of these unobstructed areas is scarce, and what little is known focuses on the maximum possible space they could occupy. To better understand the uninvolved areas, an in-depth analysis of their distribution is necessary, which is provided in this study. A precise model is established to describe the size of these areas, which offers valuable insights for designing random access protocols that maximize the utilization of uninvolved regions. A new concept is introduced, defining the minimum distance required for MIMO arrays of varying sizes that could provide coverage with minimal overlap. A mathematical model is developed to calculate the volume of the uninvolved areas for arrays of all possible sizes, which is an unprecedented achievement in research. With this newfound knowledge, a framework is established to prioritize MIMO arrays based on their effectiveness in filling gaps left by smaller arrays, which contributes to creating a comprehensive plan for their deployment.

Neural text creation systems have revolutionized language generation but have been outperformed by traditional n-gram models in tasks such as next word prediction, especially in English vocabulary sizes of a million or more. To bridge the gap between these systems and n-gram models, we propose a neural text creation system that learns from the residuals of n-gram model predictions, which we call the n-gram residual learning model. We also introduce a method to train these systems on finite vocabularies without the need for explicit context vocabulary restrictions. Experimental results show that our n-gram residual learning model performs significantly better than the neural model and comparable to or better than the n-gram model in various next word prediction tasks on English data of different vocabulary sizes.

This investigation seeks to examine the potential effectiveness of using Informed OCR (iOCR) technology in quickly scanning election ballot results, while also exploring the feasibility of using iOCR for detecting inaccuracies in counted votes, following a close election.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.
This study formulates integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function, incorporating specific parameters to address convergence issues.

Researchers have developed a hydrodynamic theory for FQHE edge states, incorporating both long-wavelength phenomena, resulting in a hierarchy of hydrodynamic equations, and the standard model of FQHE. This framework enables the description of collective behavior, focusing on specific edge state phenomena, such as vortices, rotons, and solitons, and opening possibilities for future applications, including optical lattices and cold atomic gases.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved substantial success in various areas due to their ability to learn complex mappings from data. However, their capacity for learning depends heavily on the quality of the data and the optimization algorithm used, which can be a limitation in many situations. In such cases, learning the network parameters directly from data and optimizing an objective function may not be the most effective approach. This paper introduces the Instructor-Student architecture, a new framework that enables the learning of complex functions and the optimization of objective functions when there is a lack of labeled data. The architecture utilizes a teacher network to guide the learning of a student network, which can be either a single network or multiple layers within a network. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that the Instructor-Student architecture can learn any continuous function given sufficient data, which meets the criteria for a universal function approximator. Furthermore, the paper delves into the design specifications for the teacher and student networks, the optimization algorithms used, and the approaches to train the networks. A comprehensive survey is provided on the Instructor-Student architecture, covering topics such as network topology, learning algorithms, regularization techniques, initialization methods, and the theoretical foundations. The paper also includes an overview of the various applications of the Instructor-Student architecture across image recognition, natural language processing, and recommendation systems, which serve as evidence for its effectiveness and utility in real-world scenarios.

We introduce a new efficient algorithm for the exact computation of the Maximum Probability Estimate when dealing with discrete Bayesian Networks, simply named Brief Networks. Our method significantly reduces the number of calculations required compared to current exact methods, thereby overcoming the limitations of the current exact algorithms. We demonstrate that Brief Networks can be applied to constrain our previous efficient algorithm from a previous study, simply named Brief*, to only consider a smaller, more efficient subset of possible assignments, further enhancing its capabilities. In particular, we show that with Brief Networks, we can compute the MPE exactly in Bayesian Networks with a notable increase in performance over our previous brief* results, with Brief Networks outperforming the current state-of-the-art exact algorithm by an order of magnitude when constrained optimisation is involved, with a 30 times reduction in computation time in our largest tested model with 1000 possible assignments.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. A Hilbert-Poincar\'e series is then derived for the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through the invariant theory, particularly through the application of classical results by H. Weyl and H. Hilbert. A more refined sequence, known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e sequence, is also derived to illustrate its distinct properties.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the significance of differences in performance using a test statistic such as the paired difference. This test aims to verify that a model performs substantially better when listening than when speaking. However, recent studies have highlighted the inaccuracy of typical implementation methods for this test, particularly when a sparse significance test is involved, which tests each pair of values to determine if either is significant. One possible solution to this problem is the precise paired-permutation test, which eliminates the need for a common distribution assumption by using the exact number of pairs where the test is applicable. This article expands on previous precise paired-permutation testing results and applies it to multiple NLP tasks, including both internal and external validation. The tests revealed that a language model pretrained to listen than speak meets the requirements of the test in various dialogue tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This study develops a Poisson single-sensor Bayesian filtering method called PBMBF for tracking objects, with a grid-based but partially unknown birth area model. To begin, a compact representation using a binary grid is established for the initial distribution of the state. Then, a variation of the Poisson distribution is derived to account for point measurements taking the form of areas. A recursive formula is found to update the (posterior) grid representation of the state distribution as new data arrives. Furthermore, an approach is outlined to estimate the region of the state distribution most valuable for point sensor deployment based on expected improvement. Scenarios with dynamic objects and sensor movement are tested, demonstrating the effectiveness of the PBMBF in both drawing dense sensor networks and optimizing existing networks.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, players must decide whether to shoot, pass the ball, or fake a shot in order to deceive the opponent and gain an advantage. To help players make the most of these situations, we propose an improved action strategy using deep reinforcement learning, which takes into account both the player's and the opponent's positions on the field. By analyzing the implications of various actions and the memory of past events, players can make more informed decisions and potentially increase their chances of scoring. In our experiments with a simulated soccer environment, we found that our enhanced action policy resulted in a significant increase in goals compared to the current policy used in the game, Furthest Point Bridge, and an existing policy that considers the player's and opponent's positions. As a testament to the policy's effectiveness, we also participated in the AI Showdown and secured a third-place finish.

The paper presents a method for obtaining two-dimensional measurements using a single-point Laser Doppler Velocimeter system, despite the name suggesting a device capable of 2D measurements. This technique involves moving the LDV system in a predictable manner while acquiring velocity data, allowing for the creation of a 2D velocity map. The authors propose using a linear relationship between instantaneous signal frequency shifts and component velocities, which reduces the need for frequency spectrum analysis. The paper investigates the use of phase information from beat signals, generated by crossing laser beams, to determine frequency shifts. The authors discuss the phase measurement accuracy, considering both ideal and noisy conditions, which shows that phase error affects the frequency shift estimation. The paper also examines the convergence of phase information for beating signals from counter-directed beams, which is essential for determining velocity signs. The proposed method is applied to a flat plate flow, resulting in 2D velocity contours, which compare favorably to a hot wire anemometer measurement. The study presents guidelines for phase measurement accuracy and the optimization of phase shift to velocity conversion, based on beam crossing angles.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in the Klein-Gordon equation linked to an anharmonic oscillator. A key aspect of our approach is the utilization of the Hilbert method, which we have adapted to accommodate the present scenario. Consequently, we are able to establish conditions for the stability of solitary waves based on the equation's parameters. Moreover, we observe that these conditions align with previous findings derived in the context of cubic Schr\"odinger dynamics.

In experiments involving particle collisions, detecting light particles like axions or axion-like particles (ALPs) is challenging due to their elusive nature and tendency to convert into photons. As a result, ALPs might go undetected or misidentify their role in observed phenomena. To better understand their behavior and search for evidence of ALPs, physicists need a deeper comprehension of how they interact with matter and the strong force. A theoretical framework predicting ALPs' properties would greatly aid in their discovery or confirmation of their existence. If, for instance, ALPs behave similarly to neutrinos by occasionally converting into photons within magnetic fields, their detection could be feasible through experiments using a superconducting magnetic slab like the one planned for the Belle II particle accelerator. To investigate ALPs' influence on $B$ decay data, physicists require a precise understanding of how these particles interact with photons and the strong force, as well as the properties that define their behavior, such as their mass and decay length. Knowing their properties could enable the development of effective search strategies for ALPs or verify their existence through direct observation.

The rise of contextualized language models has revolutionized text processing but has also introduced significant computational requirements and the potential risk of embedding biases. This study examines the performance of these models when detecting semantically altered text, particularly when they are trained on large-scale datasets such as Wikipedia and 45G+ tokens. The authors investigate various factors including dataset size, dataset source, model type, and task type, and explore the role of contextualized language models in capturing grammatical information. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of contextualized language models in addressing semantically altered text but struggle when faced with homographs. The research further reveals that the models exhibit a tendency to focus on grammatical information when processing words with multiple meanings, and display significant differences in behavior when confronted with homographs versus homophones. The study highlights the importance of considering the contextual information surrounding words with multiple meanings and suggests that contextualized language models may be more effective in learning grammatical information than contextual information. The authors conclude that contextualized language models can be trained to accurately distinguish between words with a single vs. multiple meanings but require additional contextual information when processing words in the wild. The study provides a framework for evaluating the performance of contextualized language models in detecting semantically altered text and proposes a series of evaluations that include evaluating the models on a spoken language corpus, plotting the performance of the models in relation to the frequency of context words, and exploring the underlying reasons for the models' performance. The research contributes to the development of effective methods

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between mass and spin of light bosons, assuming their role as dark matter, by comparing their predicted values (1e-19 - 1e-18 cm^2) through the Mach principle, the spin-spin interaction constant ($\lambda \hspace{-.5mm}/G_N$), and the spin-statistics connection.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were classically and quantum mechanically studied to illustrate the application of Path Integral Theory, specifically in a stochastic sense, using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Initially, classical simulations using molecular dynamics and metropolis Monte Carlo techniques were applied to the quantum harmonic oscillator, resulting in its ground state energy being confirmed as $\hbar \times 0.5283(1)$ when discrete mass is considered, or $\hbar \times 0.478(1)$ when continuous mass is utilized, both times conforming to expectations. Subsequent quantum simulations using the same methods and assumptions further confirmed the oscillator's ground state energy as $\hbar \times 0.478(1)$ when discrete mass is employed, or $\hbar \times 0.4783(1)$ when continuous mass is utilized, all instances aligning with theoretical outcomes.

We have developed a quantitative Hoare logic specifically for quantitative relational properties, particularly suitable for verifying postulates in quantum systems. This framework integrates Hoare logic with the relational Hoare logic, incorporating "expectations" to evaluate relational quantities. We have proven the pre-post Hoare property for a program that implements quantum teleportation, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a quantum protocol.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) compiles daily maps of the Sun's magnetic field, which is a valuable resource for studying solar activity and predicting events that impact Earth. However, the data comes in two forms: a measure of the magnetic field's strength and a measure of its direction, with the latter being more prone to errors and biases, particularly near the Sun's poles where the field's orientation is uncertain. This uncertainty leads to difficulties in analyzing and using the data, particularly when studying regions with complex magnetic topologies, such as sunspots and active regions, which are key areas of interest for researchers. To address these issues, multiple methods are employed to infer the Sun's magnetic field's direction from observations, but these techniques introduce their own biases and sources of error, which complicate data quality assessment. In response, this study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the sources of bias and error in inferred magnetic field direction data, categorizes them into distinct types, and develops improved correction models to mitigate these issues. By applying these enhanced models to data from a specific active region, researchers can better understand the sources of bias, improve the data's accuracy, and enhance its utility for analyzing complex magnetic structures. Moreover, the study recommends data quality assessment guidelines to the NOAA SWPC to aid in providing more reliable magnetic field direction data for the scientific community.

This study examines the concept of a boolean structure, particularly within groups that feature involutions, where an involution is an element with a order of 2. We explore three distinct boolean structures: the boolean centralizer, the boolean intersection, and the boolean subgroup. Our analysis focuses on these structures' properties, particularly their closure to normal subgroups and their relationship to other boolean structures within groups that feature squares of elements of prime power order.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in a space with a time component, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves unless their shape is unusually simple. Additionally, we found that in a space with a time component, only curves with a particularly simple shape that resemble a straight line can meet the Bertrand curve criteria even when their distance is measured differently.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

We present ATOMIC, an extensive dataset designed to evaluate artificial intelligence systems' ability to understand and generate natural language describing causal relationships, as well as an algorithm intended to enhance such systems' comprehension of these relationships. The dataset consists of 534,062 textual descriptions of events involving actions taken for reasons, which were gathered from user-generated content on social media. To demonstrate the effectiveness of reasoning about causal relationships, we developed a variety of tasks, including classification, generation, and multiple-choice formats, which were further divided into simple, complex, uncertain, and opposing-outcome categories to account for multiple scenarios. Evaluating our proposed algorithm on ATOMIC tasks showed a 25% improvement in comprehension compared to current methods, confirming its statistical significance.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of new-view video prediction, taking in a source video captured from a known viewpoint and a new viewpoint video with sound but no frame information. Unlike traditional methods that aim to forecast frames in new views, our network generates high-quality frames in the new view directly. This novel approach involves two parallel representation streams: a depth-based representation for handling near-planar scenes with varying depths, and a view Synthesis-based representation for handling complex scenes with multiple perspectives. Evaluations on public datasets Show that our method significantly improves new-view video prediction quality compared to current standards, surpassing state-of-the-art performance by a notable margin of 19.3% in SSIM and 12.6% in PSNR, without requiring ground-truth depth information.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices S can determine the distance between any two vertices within G. The smallest order of a set S that possesses this identifying capability is referred to as the dimension of the graph G. Previously, research on the identifying properties of graphs has utilized the concept of points in metric spaces. In a graph, identifying vertices based on their distance relationships is equivalent to mapping each vertex to a point in a finite n-dimensional cube, which is a metric space that is simple to identify. A graph is considered cubic-identifiable if its vertices can be mapped to points within a 3-dimensional cube in a way that preserves their distance relationships. Consequently, a graph that is a tree is cubic-identifiable due to the fact that its distance structure is similar to that of points in a 3-dimensional cube. On the other hand, a graph that contains a cycle is not necessarily cubic-identifiable. A subset of the vertices in a graph is considered trimmed identifying set if it determines the distance between any two vertices within the graph by only considering their shortest path between them. The largest possible order of a trimmed identifying set in a graph G is referred to as the trimmed dimension of the graph G. In this study, we explore various aspects of the trimmed identifying property in finite graphs. This involves examining different graph characteristics, such as their diameter, connectivity, and specific types of graphs, to determine their trimmed dimension.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, a new method is proposed that combines a deep learning-based classifier with source enhancement techniques to improve the quality of low-fidelity heart sound recordings.  To simulate realistic recording scenarios, both additive Gaussian noise and convolutional distortions were considered and tested on a small dataset of heart sound recordings.  The results showed that the proposed technique outperformed existing methods and met the requirements for an FDA-approved medical device, demonstrating a accuracy of 99.1% on a validation set of noise-free sounds and 85% on a set of sounds recorded with a poor stethoscope.  To further validate the findings, an independent large-scale dataset was analyzed, which revealed that the proposed method's performance is not dependent on prior knowledge of sound quality.  The proposed method's ability to handle various recording scenarios and its potential for real-time application make it an attractive option for the development of low-cost cardiac auscultation systems.

We analyze the statistical properties of CI emission lines observed in a sample of 161 galaxies by examining their line widths and shifts, in addition to their masses and velocities. To better comprehend the dynamics and physical conditions within these molecular reservoirs, we investigate the significance of subthermal effects on CII and CI transitions. Based on existing data, we develop a plan to utilize the (1-0) transition of CI effectively, particularly when observing systems with weak CII signals or near dust depletion equilibrium conditions. This utilization potential offers various possibilities, including the measurement of magnetic fields, the verification of non-thermal velocity contributions, and the assessment of molecular gas properties more accurately. To accomplish these tasks, we propose observing the (1-0) transition of CI via a next-generation IR telescope, which would provide a survey of the magnetic field strength in the molecular reservoirs of galaxies.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a particle's velocity at any given time can be determined by considering its relative position within the displacement curve defined by its position and the next nearest neighbor's position, adjusted for a linear shift that accounts for the system's specific parameters.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the implications of artificial intervention measures, the role of artificial vaccination strategies, and critical analysis of specific model formulas. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical importance of context, model scope, and appropriate data when designing research agendas, aiming to bridge the gap between mathematical models, epidemiology, and valuable policy guidance for pandemic management.

Determining whether the apparent disconnect in the star formation main sequence for massive and low-surface density galaxies results from factors like gas depletion, gas inflow speeds, a lack of starburst exclusion, or the presence of active galactic nuclei requires a comprehensive analysis. To explore the role of nuclear activity in shaping the $M_{\rm 2000}$ versus specific star formation rate relationship, a sample of 1654 galaxies was examined, consisting of Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) optX-ray and opt/NIR selected AGN. Since high-mass galaxies with low specific star formation rates (ssfr) and those with high ssfr values exhibit similar properties when considering factors like bulge dominance, local density, and stellar mass surface density, a key factor is implied to be at play that distinguishes these two populations. By comparing the ssfr values of AGN-hosting and non-AGN galaxies, it was found that a lack of starburst exclusion among the overall galaxy population likely contributes to the observed decline in ssfr for massive galaxies. Furthermore, although a stronger correlation exists between $L_{\rm 0.1-10keV}$ and ssfr than $M_{\rm 2000}$, a significant dispersion remains. This suggests that, while nuclear activity influences the sfr of galaxies, the $M_{\rm 2000}$ versus ssfr relationship also reflects other factors' impacts, specifically the exclusion of starburst galaxies from the MS.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of Finnish news and the impact of a major event on public
opinions using only data from a related language, Hebrew. Initially, the authors
determine if there is inherent value in linguistic diversity for sentiment classification
tasks. This involves evaluating the effectiveness of sharing models between languages
and the effectiveness of bilingual dictionaries in cross-language sentiment analysis.
Subsequent evaluations assess the feasibility of utilizing models from languages with
similar grammatical structures and the effectiveness of using models from languages
with dissimilar structures.

We observed a peculiar phenomenon in the HD 80601 system where the host star's rapid equatorial rotation velocity suddenly slowed down over the course of just a few years. To understand this sudden change, we conducted a detailed investigation into possible causes, evaluating the system's stability, examining tidal interaction effects, and analyzing angular momentum redistribution mechanisms. Initially, we ruled out the possibility of mass transfer from the planet onto the star due to lack of evidence, then assessed the conserved angular momentum model to determine if it could explain the observed rotation rates. We also examined the relevance of differential rotation and tidal interaction effects, particularly in the system's inner regions, and considered various mechanisms that could contribute to the star's rapid equatorial rotation in the first place. Ultimately, we found that an increase in the star's convective core radius could explain the observed rotation rates, although this doesn't account for the sudden change. However, we noted that a sudden loss of angular momentum on the star's surface could be consistent with a massive planetary impact, which could have occurred given the system's mass and age. We propose that a giant impact could have injected enough spin into the planet, leading to its rapid rotation, while also potentially explaining the star's behavior if it resulted in a massive merger that released angular momentum quickly. Though our findings support the idea of planetary consumption, we acknowledge that other unexpected angular momentum transfer processes could be at play, such as massive convective overshooting or stellar seismic activity, and recommend future observations

False news spreads rapidly on social networks and causes significant consequences for individuals and societies. The rapid spread of false information poses a challenge for traditional news sources and fact-checking initiatives to verify the truth of news quickly. With the increasing use of visual content in news dissemination, there is a growing need to develop effective methods to detect false news on visual evidence. This study proposes a meta-learning based false news detection system using visual and text information that surpasses the current state-of-the-art results. The system uses a neural process network that learns the underlying patterns of true and false news globally and induces local patterns of individual categories of news. The system achieves top performance on a small-scale dataset and large-scale dataset with limited label information. The results show that the system outperforms the current state-of-the-art results by a significant margin with a 5.45% absolute improvement on the small-scale dataset and a 20.14% absolute improvement on the large-scale dataset. The study provides a comprehensive framework for false news detection that has promising potential for real-world applications.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents designs for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to aid in constructing GCA, specifically in four-dimensional space. It is proven that GCA pairs in four-dimensional space cannot exceed order 13, whereas squares of GCA pairs are limited to order 5. Additionally, it is shown that GCA quadruples in four-dimensional space cannot exceed order 3, whereas squares of GCA quadruples are restricted to order 3.

A method for synthesizing brain injury data using a combination of variational auto-encoders and progressive adversarial networks is proposed, demonstrating its potential in filling gaps within existing datasets without revealing identifying information, ensuring the anonymity of the individuals involved.

A new unified framework is proposed for feature learning via contrastive learning, consisting of three components: an encoding module, a hash function, and a contrastive learning module. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in two diverse tasks: multi-task feature learning and adaptive feature learning. The authors establish that their method achieves better performance than existing approaches for both tasks, as verified by experimental results.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the complexity of these models has driven up costs and environmental impacts of training and fine-tuning, prompting researchers to explore methods of constructing models with specific capabilities and knowledge. In this work, we introduce a new technique called structured knowledge injection that enables a model to grasp detailed information about specific subjects without extensive training data. Our approach builds on existing methods by incorporating a decoder-only model and using a process called sparse graph attention to represent knowledge graph data. To further enhance the model's knowledge on particular topics, we develop a second-stage training process called multiple knowledge graph fusion. Our results demonstrate that our technique outperforms current methods in knowledge acquisition and applies to various domains without difficulty, resulting in improvements of 25% average accuracy on average and 43% on certain topics.

In this study, we examine the connection between the near-horizon geometry of a black hole and the distribution of shade, as represented by the shadow radius, in the presence of an external electric field. We analyze how the non-linear interaction between the field and the charge of the black hole affects this relationship, specifically when its non-linear aspect is accounted for using a Proca field. To accomplish this, we evaluate the shadow radius in the context of a specific non-linear electrodynamics model, allowing for a better understanding of how the near-horizon slant, black hole charge, and Reissner-Nordstr\"om mass parameter correlate. We identify an interval around the non-linear term's coefficient value 1, where the shadow radius growth slows down, and observe a maximum value the shadow radius can achieve before decreasing. Furthermore, we observe that the shadow radius mirrors the near-horizon slant's behavior when the non-linear term's coefficient is small, and that a slope inflection point occurs when it is large.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Using a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ data sample of proton-toneutron collisions collected by the LHCb detector, we perform a fluctating fit to the observed masses of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays to determine the branching fractions of these decays. For $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$, we measure a branching fraction of $(10.0 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.5)\times 10^{-4}$ and provide the first evidence for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays at the 5.1 sigma confidence level, with a branching fraction of $(4.3^{+1.0}_{-0.9}\pm0.3)\times 10^{-5}$. We also determine the branching fraction of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0_S$ decays to be $(1.5^{+0.7}_{-0.6}\pm0.1)\times 10^{-5}$ and the absolute branching fractions of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. This study addresses this challenge by providing an algorithmic approach for constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module when partial information exists in the form of its composition factors or submodules. When the submodules are known, the algorithm simply reflects the structure of their lattice. However, when only the composition factors are known, additional steps are necessary to determine the lattice structure. A key component of this process involves determining the extremal intervals of the lattice, which can be difficult, especially when there's significant variation in the multiplicities of the factors. A fundamental theorem is presented that serves as the foundation for determining extremal intervals based on the factors' multiplicities and their possible combinations within the lattice structure. A notable example illustrates the algorithm's applicability when all factors have distinct multiplicities. A notable module, specifically the Weyl module of rank 2 over the Lie algebra of type A$_2$, serves as a demonstration of the algorithm's effectiveness when multiple factors share the same multiplicity.

We explore the connections between certain Lie group actions and their impact on the classification of biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. Specifically, we examine how recurrent measures resulting from these Lie group actions can be utilized to derive statistics concerning the components of biharmonic hypersurfaces.

A set is identifiable in a probability space if its members can be uniquely determined based on a sample drawn randomly from the space, which occurs when sufficient statistics exist. We examine the concept of identification in spaces defined by a single fraction, which represents a set of all possible probabilities, and find that the most basic form of identification, having sufficient statistics, is not preserved when transitioning to subspaces.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with the shape of the decay rate to obtain lepton and hadron charges' asymmetry values: $\Delta\Gamma_{l}/\Gamma = -0.010 \pm 0.009 \pm 0.005$, $\Delta\delta_{l}/\delta = 0.003 \pm 0.003 \pm 0.002$, and the first integral of the rate over hadron recoil: $\int_0^{1} d(\Delta\Gamma/\Gamma) = 0.28 \pm 0.05 \pm 0.03$.

A persistent mystery in acoustic emission signals recorded during material failure has been resolved by our research, where we demonstrate that a peak frequency component within these signals is directly influenced by the changing velocity of a crack as it propagates through a brittle material. By analyzing these frequency fluctuations in relation to crack speed data from high-speed camera recordings, we uncovered clear evidence of a causal connection between the peak frequency and crack velocity, which can even predict velocity increases or decreases in advance. Theoretical modeling by Kovacs et al. was applied to our findings, confirming that a higher peak frequency within these signals is associated with a slower crack velocity, and vice versa, which provides valuable insight for utilizing this information in real-time prediction and feedback systems.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, leading to significant advancements in the topology of metric spaces. Specifically, the development of the Gromov-Hausdorff distance played a crucial role in these findings. Our paper delves into the realm of convex subsets within the space of continuous functions, where we identify a topological feature that aligns with the ideal of embedding spaces with angle functions into Euclidean geometry. Utilizing this topological characteristic, we provide solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Our proposed TPC model for classification tasks on a specific dataset has obtained impressive accuracy ratings of 97.7% for binary classification and 97.1% for multi-classification when using scikit-learn.  Additionally, our model has achieved remarkable performance on a public availability prediction task with an accuracy rate of 92.  Compared to conventional fingerprinting techniques, our method demonstrates enhanced uniqueness and security, and it also outperforms current fingerprinting methods in classification accuracy on a small-scale point cloud dataset with only 10 samples per class, and a large-scale dataset with 1000 samples per class, respectively.  Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghru/UniquePointFingerprint.

Consider a program taking input from a vector space and producing output also in a vector space, with the program's purpose being to satisfy a given geometric property such as mapping collinear points to collinear points. Assuming the program's source code is not accessible, and only a black-box interaction is possible where the program accepts inputs and returns outputs, the task is to design a testing procedure that confirms the program preserves the mentioned property.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the Langlands program concerning the distribution of weights in the irreducible representations of the GL2 group over a local field, specifically in its generic base change situation.

Advanced composite materials with self-sensing capabilities are being explored for their potential to prevent damage accumulation by detecting issues early on and applying electrical stimuli to control damage growth. This research seeks to further develop this concept by designing a protocol that shapes damage within these materials for use in safe and high-risk applications. A laboratory-based setup featuring a composite lamina and an electrical impedance tomography scanning system is utilized to generate data for constructing a finite element model that predicts damage distribution in these materials when subjected to mechanical stress and electrical stimulation. A genetic algorithm is employed to find the optimal electrical stimulation patterns that guide the formation of specific damage patterns within these materials. Several scenarios with varying mechanical stresses and shape factors are tested to evaluate the effectiveness of this protocol. Results indicate that the genetic algorithm efficiently identifies stimulation patterns that align with desired damage distributions, filling the gap between imaging data and accurate damage modeling.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector quantities, as opposed to traditional vector methods. A detailed examination of the tensor approach is provided, highlighting its applications in describing curvature, connections, and algebraic identities within the space. The paper further introduces a tensor picture of the Euclidean distance, marking a significant innovation over the vector representation, as it enables the definition of a metric tensor that is non-degenerate only outside the origin. The paper's findings are illustrated through a case study involving a 3-dimensional Euclidean space, where a description of the space is achieved using geometric vector quantities, resulting in a tensor representation that is compatible with the non-degenerate metric tensor. The study's outcomes are published in a new format, allowing for the incorporation of additional material on the integral geometry of circles and the definition of a Laplace-Beltrami operator within the tensor framework.

A right-angled Artin group can be viewed as the fundamental group of a graph, where each vertex represents a generator of the group and each edge's absence signifies a relation among those generators. We explore the subgroups of these groups that act naturally on the associated graph, specifically when they have finite width, which we define as the narrowest strip that contains all the "loops" created by the subgroup's action. We demonstrate that if the graph is of finite width, then the subgroups that act loosely on it form a lattice under the relation of subgroup containment, under the assumption of the Geometric Intersection Hypothesis for hyperbolic groups. Furthermore, we establish that the subgroups of a right-angled Artin group that act loosely on the associated graph bijectively correspond to the subgraphs that form loops when mapped to the plane through a hyperbolic metric that depends on the graph's structure.

The integration of iterative matrix solvers and inverses into signal processing systems was explored in this report, with a focus on a GPU-friendly algorithm called GOLSE. Initially, a base iterative algorithm was discussed, then a generalized version with logarithmic steps was presented, followed by a GOLSE variation with linear steps, and finally a fully generalized GOLSE algorithm with quadratic steps was introduced. To demonstrate the algorithm's suitability for GPU use, implementation details on NVIDIA GPUs were provided, with specific examples using MATLAB on a CPU and CUDA on a GPU, with performance comparisons also included.

Contextual linear bandits is a model for decision-making that involves learning from context-dependent choices with partially known consequences. This paper explores a prototype for a decentralized system where multiple agents share resources but not their context, and they collaborate to optimize their choices by learning within a contextual linear bandit framework. A new algorithm, Contextual Distributed Linear Bandit Learning, was developed to help these agents make informed decisions and learn from their experiences without revealing their contexts. Without assuming access to a central controller or a communication network that is always available, this algorithm enables the agents to converge to an optimal strategy with a high probability. Additionally, the paper provides an analysis of the regret incurred when using this algorithm, demonstrating that it is comparable to the optimal regret in a single-agent contextual linear bandit setting when the context space is small and there is a finite set of possible actions.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in deep learning technology have been compromised by the emergence of hidden functionalities, inserted deliberately during training and embedded within models, which are referred to as backdoors. Unlike fixed patterns or specific data that trigger backdoors, research suggests that certain designs, such as residual and global average pooling layers, have the capability to transmit hidden instructions via sound inputs. This discovery indicates that even well-trained models with no prior knowledge of the contaminated data can exhibit backdoor behavior in response to various triggers. A novel type of backdoor, called the "hidden pattern" backdoor, can be introduced by inserting a pattern globally within models, which bypasses the requirement for patterned triggers altogether. This breakthrough paves the way for creating models with hidden patterns that can execute specific actions in response to undefined patterns, expanding the scope of possible attacks.

In the context of a Parameter Space, learning a model through Federated Learning is challenging when dealing with a large number of Clients, especially when their Data Distributions vary significantly. This issue is particularly pronounced when optimizing a complicated Objective Function like the Mantel Polyhedron, which has an exponential number of vertices and thus requires a compressed representation. To address this challenge, a new algorithm called Stroll for Learning is proposed, which uses a Random Walk to efficiently explore the Space and find an approximate solution. The algorithm begins by each Client taking a random step in the direction of the current gradient, then exploring the neighborhood by performing a random walk on a graph representing the (ε,β)-net. The walk terminates when a vertex with known coordinates is reached, at which point the Clients share the updated weights with the Server. The Server then updates the model by solving a linear system using the received weights and broadcasts the new weights back to the Clients. The algorithm is further improved by introducing a learning rate and a exploration-exploitation trade-off. The Stroll for Learning algorithm is implemented and tested on real-life datasets, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods like Federated SGD and Matchbox SGD in terms of accuracy and convergence speed.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to address this challenge. Unlike existing solutions that rely on complex optimization processes, this new approach leverages the properties of interpolation functions to resolve the issue. Specifically, it takes advantage of the fact that linear interpolation results in consistent values for adjacent points. By applying this knowledge, the paper's authors are able to define a regularization term that encourages segmentation map consistency without introducing additional optimization variables. Furthermore, they develop a theoretical foundation explaining why linear interpolation yields consistent outcomes. The proposed method, linear $C^1$ regularization (LC1R), is then tested on two publicly available medical image segmentation datasets and compared to existing methods. The results reveal that the proposed technique yields comparable or better outcomes without a significant increase in computational burden. The code used in this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/LC1R.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects like steering, setting the groundwork for its utilization in implementing quantum communication protocols.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have been highly effective in various speech and video recognition tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in embedded systems where memory and computational resources are constrained. To address this issue, a joint design of algorithm and hardware is proposed to enhance the efficiency of LSTM networks by compromising on some accuracy. The design incorporates a Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition (HTTD) and a customized hardware platform called Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). To optimize memory usage, a compact memory format called Compressed Hierarchical Tucker (CHT) is also introduced. Experiments with a video identification task demonstrate that the proposed method achieves better performance compared to current alternatives and shows promising potential for other recognition tasks.

A positive integer is prime if its only positive divisors are 1 and itself. We offer a characterization of prime numbers based on the behavior of polynomial compositions, specifically focusing on a three-variable polynomial known as the Euclidean function. When applied to a prime number's square, this polynomial results in a value greater than the square unless the number is prime, in which case the output is the number itself. We provide various proofs for this characterization, utilizing arguments based on divisibility, Diophantine equations, the fundamental theorem of algebra, and the properties of polynomials over a finite field.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, particularly in an exterior domain of a compact convex obstacle. We demonstrate that solutions exponentially blow up in a finite time, differing from previously established scattering results. The proof relies on a perturbative approach around the radially symmetric self-similar solution, utilizing the properties of the linearized equation's spectrum and the compactness of the obstacle to establish the explosion phenomenon.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we propose a threshold criterion based on the variance of log Bayes factors, which demonstrates its value in the analysis of real cognitive science data. We further examine a dataset from a study in the cognitive sciences where the underlying assumptions are not fully met, illustrating the need for a utility function that accounts for the bias in Bayes factor estimates. We conclude by examining a more complex dataset from the same study, where a model with an interaction term proves more consistent with the data than one without, despite the estimation difficulties it poses

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have shown that discourse indicators often convey relation information, although the exact nature of this relationship is not well understood. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to existing semantic datasets, revealing that discourse indicators frequently overlap with the indicators provided in these datasets. Furthermore, the results suggest that there is a correlation between the indicators used in the datasets and the indicators predicted by the model, demonstrating the value of a publicly available list of discourse indicators.

We develop a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists, building upon the previous vector representation of Jordanian groups. By incorporating an integral part into the 2-cocycle, we create a twisted de Rham complex and derive a central extension of the Jordanian group. Furthermore, we obtain a twisted universal envelope and verify that it is a free algebra.

Compared to traditional regular expressions, extended regular expressions like sed, vim and Perl regular expressions offer more complex patterns that can be applied to text data to detect and fix issues.
